newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir death toll is big, unanswered question.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir death toll is big, unanswered question.

text.p: The fate of four Western hostages in Kashmir is one of the many unanswered questions in the seven-year-old separatist revolt in the mountainous Himalayan region.
Just as much uncertainty surrounds the number of deaths in an armed rebellion that exploded in 1990.
Hundreds, perhaps thousands, of Kashmiris remain unaccounted for, and authorities themselves differ on the exact death toll.
The government of India's Jammu and Kashmir state has an official estimate, but it is widely disputed, even by other authorities.

"Until the end of May 1997, the total number of people killed during the last seven years is 17,630, which includes militants and security force personnel also," the state government's spokesman K.B. Jandial told Reuters.
Police say the toll is higher.

"We have reports that hundreds of youth are missing and many more died on inaccessible snow-clad mountains while crossing over to Pakistan-occupied Kashmir or while returning after receiving arms training, so the toll can go higher," a senior police officer said.

Pakistan controls one third of the Himalayan region and stakes a claim over the rest. Islamabad denies India's claim that it arms and trains militants who cross into Kashmir to fight for independence or merger with Pakistan.
Kashmir's leading separatist group, the All Parties Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference, says more than 50,000 people have died in insurgency-related violence since 1990.

"According to our rough estimates, at least 52,000 people died during the last eight years in Kashmir," said Firdous Asmi, head of the Institute of Kashmir Studies, a human rights group in the state's summer capital, Srinagar.
The Jammu and Kashmir Peace Foundation, a non-governmental organisation, says 50,000 people have died.
The state's chief minister, Farooq Abdullah, agrees. In numerous speeches he has said more than 50,000 people have died in the rebellion.
